title: Two Different Problems: Mistakes vs. Errors
brief: Open by establishing why the distinction matters for teachers, drawing directly on the source's glossary definitions: a mistake is 'the result of inattention or carelessness, rather than incomplete learning,' while an error reflects 'patterns in production that show incomplete or incorrect learning.' Use the source's guideline that teachers should first 'understand why the error occurred — did the student not know how to produce the correct language, or did they make a careless mistake?' to show how the distinction shapes the teacher's next move. Illustrate with a brief classroom scenario (e.g., a student who writes 'he go' once in a rushed draft versus one who consistently omits the third-person -s) to make the conceptual difference concrete. Keep correction technique itself minimal — that is covered in the companion section.

title: Interlanguage: The Learner's Developing System
brief: Introduce interlanguage in plain, accessible terms as the evolving, rule-governed system a learner builds on the way to the target language — a system that is neither the learner's first language nor the target language but something in between. Anchor the explanation in the source's definition of error as evidence of 'incomplete or incorrect learning' and the source's framing of 'trial and error' as 'learning by trying new or different language, taking risks, and learning from errors or mistakes.' Explain that systematic errors — patterns that recur across learners at similar stages — are the visible surface of this internal system, not random failures. Emphasise that interlanguage is dynamic: it shifts as learners receive input and feedback, which is why the source stresses that 'making mistakes helps them learn' and that teachers should 'tell students that making mistakes helps them learn.'

title: Errors as Evidence of Learning
brief: Reframe errors positively as diagnostic data rather than failures, drawing on the source's explicit instruction to 'encourage student learning through positive feedback' and to 'help students to be successful and confident' by treating mistakes as 'part of the learning process.' Use the source's description of the trial-and-error process — students 'taking risks and learning from errors or mistakes' — to show that producing errors is an active, necessary stage of acquisition. Bring in the verified research to support the claim that feedback on those errors genuinely advances learning: both Lyster & Saito (2010) and Li (2010) confirm through meta-analysis that corrective feedback has significant effects on acquisition, meaning the errors students produce are not just inevitable but teachable moments with measurable payoff. Close by connecting this positive framing to the source's affective domain guidance: creating 'a positive atmosphere for risk-taking so students feel comfortable trying to use the language.'

title: Diagnosing What Went Wrong: Types of Error
brief: Walk teachers through the diagnostic process the source outlines: once a teacher has established that a production problem is a genuine error (not a careless mistake), the next step is to 'determine the type of error — grammar, vocabulary, or pragmatic in nature (inappropriate usage).' Use the source's three-domain framework — linguistic, communicative, and affective — to show that errors can occur at different levels and that the type of error determines the appropriate response. Draw on the source's glossary definition of 'diagnose' — 'to determine exactly what kind of mistake or error the student is making and what might be the cause of the error' — as the organising concept for this section. Provide brief illustrative examples for each error type (grammatical, lexical, pragmatic) drawn from the source's own categories, keeping the focus on identification rather than correction technique.

title: Patterns Across Learners: Using Error Analysis to Plan Teaching
brief: Shift from diagnosing individual errors to identifying patterns across a class, using the source's guidance to 'deal with errors the whole class is making' separately from individual errors. Explain how recurring errors — the same grammatical gap, the same pragmatic misstep — signal a shared stage in the learners' interlanguage and therefore a shared teaching need. Draw on the source's answer-key example of delayed feedback: 'if many students had the same language problem or were making mistakes on one part of the content, the teacher could have the whole class work on it after the activity was completed.' Connect this to the source's broader principle that it is important to 'understand the nature of an error in order to determine whether and how to use corrective feedback,' and that teachers must decide 'whether the error is important enough to correct' or whether fluency is the priority for a given task. End by framing error analysis as a planning tool: what students consistently get wrong tells the teacher what to teach next.

title: Formative Feedback and the Diagnostic Mindset
brief: Bring the unit together by situating the mistake-error distinction and error analysis within the source's concept of formative feedback — feedback that is 'continuous,' given 'at all stages throughout the learning period,' and used 'to determine what has been learned so far and what still needs work.' Contrast this briefly with summative feedback (given at the end of a unit to measure achievement) to clarify why ongoing diagnosis matters more for shaping instruction. Use the source's action-plan guidance — 'determine what the student's problem really is' and 'maintain student focus on the language goal of the session or activity' — to give teachers a practical mindset: every error is a data point that informs the next instructional decision. Close with the source's reminder that the goal of this diagnostic work is ultimately affective as well as linguistic: teachers who understand errors can give feedback that builds confidence rather than discouraging learners.
